political_impact.text: The order directed fortification work on Corregidor to start once the landowners gave written consent, on an island where the Army had been building batteries since 1904.
political_impact.source: Presidential Executive Orders (1944), vol. 1, p. 72, entry 763½

political_impact.text: The work fit a coast-defense program Congress had already funded and the public broadly supported, and it drew no recorded controversy.

legacy.text: Corregidor held out under Japanese bombardment from Bataan until General Wainwright asked for terms late on May 6, 1942.
A combined parachute and amphibious assault retook the island beginning February 16, 1945; MacArthur returned for the flag-raising on March 2.

today.name: Fort Mills batteries, Corregidor
today.note: The fort and its batteries survive as war memorials.

uncertain: The operative text of Executive Order 763½ has not been read; only the 1944 catalog summary is available.

political_impact.text: The Bureau of Biological Survey administered the reservation, sharing the cost of warden protection with the National Association of Audubon Societies.
political_impact.source: Robertson, The Terns of the Dry Tortugas (1964), p. 27

political_impact.text: Under warden protection begun in 1903, the Bird Key sooty-tern colony grew from roughly 5,000 adults to an estimated 18,858 in 1907 and about 40,000 by 1909.

legacy.text: The colony reached something like 80,000 to 100,000 breeding adults around 1917.
Hurricanes in 1910 and 1919 stripped Bird Key's vegetation, and the island eroded until by mid-1935 it was a sandbar; it was not destroyed by the 1935 Labor Day hurricane.
The terns moved to nearby Bush Key, where up to 80,000 sooty terns and 4,500 brown noddies nest, the only significant colony of either in the United States.

today.name: Dry Tortugas National Park
today.note: Proclamation 2112 replaced the bird reservation with Fort Jefferson National Monument in 1935; the monument became a national park in 1992.

later_actions.text: Franklin Roosevelt's Proclamation 2112 created Fort Jefferson National Monument and expressly revoked Executive Order 779.
Fort Jefferson National Monument was enlarged.
Congress redesignated the monument Dry Tortugas National Park.

reception.text: The San Francisco Call reported that Representatives Knowland and Kahn had pressed the President for a holiday in the city's federal offices on the day the fleet arrived.

political_impact.text: The holiday was extended to the federal offices in Oakland, Alameda and Berkeley, and the San Francisco post office closed for the day.

related.note: Three weeks later Roosevelt excused Civil and Spanish War veterans for a reinterment parade.

uncertain: Whether Executive Order 789 is the original San Francisco holiday order or the version extended to the East Bay cities cannot be told without its text.

legacy.text: The Alaska telegraph reservations reverted as wireless and, later, the telephone made the old military cable obsolete.
